summary: Five-lens visual review of a built V15 chapter, with skeptic verification of serious findings

confirmed.description: Marthanda Varma is off-model in his first war-hall panel. He has loose, shoulder-length curly hair with no knot and no earrings. That matches neither the bible's war-hall look (bare-headed, hair in a side knot above the left ear) nor his own look in 5.5, 6.1 to 6.5 and 7.2 to 7.5, where he has a gathered knot and gold ear drops. With loose curly hair and a thick curled moustache, he reads like a bare-headed Nagoji, and he sits in the same frame as the real Nagoji.
confirmed.evidence: In the selected frame page-05-panel-03-v05.png, the seated figure on the dais has loose wavy black hair to the nape and a bare earlobe. In 5.5 (right edge) and 7.4 the same king has a high knot and gold ear drops. CONTINUITY.md line 76 says war-hall scenes are 'bare-headed with his hair in a side knot above his left ear'. The V13 varma-v1 sheet shows drop earrings.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed. I zoomed into panel 5.3 on page-05.png (the seated figure on the dais, at about x 280 to 560 and y 1680 to 1900 at full resolution). Varma has loose, curly black hair down to his nape and over his ears. There is no knot and no visible ear drop. Script 5.3 (CHAPTER-12-SCRIPT.md line 161) asks for him "bare-headed, his hair in a side knot above his left ear". The CONTINUITY.md row "12 @5-" (the informal coastal war hall) says the same.

One panel later, in 5.5, the same king has a high gathered knot and gold ear drops. That jump inside a single scene is a real continuity break. Hair this loose and curly, with the thick curled moustache, also matches Nagoji's bare-headed V13 sheet (nagoji-v2.png) more than Varma's.

I am rating it major, not blocker. In 5.3 he is still clearly the king: he sits on the dais against the cushion, wears layered gold necklaces, armlets and a gold-bordered mundu, and has the spear at his right hand. Nagoji is in the same frame but in his rust-red turban and sash at the back, so a reader will not mix the two up. The problem is local: one head in one panel is off-model and needs redrawing.

confirmed.description: The left caption box ('And now, without knowing it...') covers the captive's torso, hands and the iron at his wrists. In the printed panel, Chanda Sahib is only a turban and beard in shadow, with nothing to show he is a prisoner. The script depends on this panel reading as 'the rider fallen', and the manacles are what carry that.
confirmed.evidence: The selected frame page-08-panel-03-v01.png shows heavy wrist cuffs and a chain across his lap. In renders/r2/page-08.png the caption box starts just below his beard and hides everything from the chest down.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this on renders/r2/page-08.png. In the zoomed crop of panel 8.3, the captive shows only from the turban to the top of his shoulders. The top edge of the left caption box ("And now, without knowing it...") sits just below his beard and covers his whole torso, his lap, his hands and the iron at his wrists. No cuff or chain shows anywhere in the printed panel.

The selected frame page-08-panel-03-v01.png does draw heavy wrist cuffs and a chain across his lap, at about frame y 550-680. In the page's crop and scale that falls entirely under the caption.

The script requires "iron at his wrists" for this panel (8.3). The adaptation notes rely on the captive reading as "the rider fallen", and he never shows his face. Without the manacles, the only things that mark him as a prisoner are his soiled jama and the missing turban jewel, which are hard to see at print size. On their own they do not say "captive".

The right caption box also hides most of the coin counting on the cloth before him. Only a hand and a few coins show. So both script props that tell this story are covered: the iron and the counted coin.

Nothing in the bible or the script allows this, and it is too large a loss to dismiss at print size.

It is major, not a blocker, because the captive is still on the panel and the second caption says "capture", so the beat survives in the text. The fix is local: move the two captions into the large empty band of dark tent canvas at the top of the panel, so the wrists, chain and coin cloth show.

confirmed.description: Varma's hair is wrong for the informal war hall and changes from panel to panel. The bible row for 12 @5- wants a bare head with the hair in a side knot above the LEFT ear. In 5.3 he has short, loose, curly hair with no knot at all, which makes him look like a younger, different man than the Varma in 5.5 on the same page, who has a high knot at the back of the crown.
confirmed.evidence: 5.3: hair loose in curls to the neck, no knot. 5.5: a tied knot high at the back of the head. 6.1 and 6.5 (from behind): a crown bun with long curly hair hanging loose to the shoulders. Nowhere in pages 5 to 7 is it a side knot above the left ear.

verdict.reason:
The problem is real. Page 5, panel 5.3 does not match the script or the bible. Both say he should be bare-headed with his hair in a side knot above the left ear. The script's own 5.3 description repeats this, and so does the bible row "12 @5-".

What the art shows:
- **5.3:** I zoomed into the native 300 DPI crop. The man on the dais has a loose mop of curls down to the nape, with no knot or tie anywhere. That makes him look younger and softer than the V13 varma-v1 face.
- **5.5 (just below on the same page):** his hair is pulled back into a tied knot high on the back of the crown, with long hair hanging behind.
- **6.3, 6.4, 6.5, 7.2, 7.4 and 7.5:** all keep the same tied knot at the back or crown. So 5.3 is the only panel that breaks the pattern.

Why it is visible at print size: his head in 5.3 is only about 4 mm tall, but the curly mop is easy to see at 1:1. In 6.4, where he is a background figure of about the same size, the knot reads clearly. A reader going from 5.3 down to 5.5 sees two different hairstyles on the same page.

Why major and not blocker: his identity still comes through from the dais seat, the gold necklaces, the armband, the moustache and the spear beside him. It is a localized hair and costume error.

The reviewer's wider point, that none of pages 5 to 7 shows a true side knot above the left ear, is weaker. The back-crown knot in 5.5 through 7.5 sits behind and above the left ear and is consistent from panel to panel, so it should not be treated as a separate defect. The fix is to redraw 5.3 with the same knot used in 5.5 to 7.5.

confirmed.description: The ola changes form within the page. In 5.2 and 5.4 it is a thick bundle of palm leaves tied with cord, and 6.1 shows the same bundle being handed over. In 5.5 Ramayyan lowers a single thin, pale, paper-like sheet covered in lines of pseudo-script. That breaks prop continuity and the no-writing rule.
confirmed.evidence: 5.4: a dark leaf bundle with its cord still wrapped round it. 5.5: one flat cream sheet held in both hands, with rows of faint writing marks across it. 6.1: the tied bundle again. 6.3 also shows a single leaf with pseudo-writing (lesser).

verdict.reason:
I checked this in zoomed crops. The prop does change shape, but the problem is smaller than reported, so I rate it minor, not major.

**What the art shows:**
- **5.4:** a dark bundle of leaves with the cord still tied round it.
- **5.5:** a short, wide, cream slip held in both hands. It is shaped like a piece of paper, not a palm leaf.
- **6.1:** the tied bundle again, being handed to Varma.
- **6.3:** a long, narrow, brown single leaf, which looks right for a palm leaf.

So within three panels the ola goes from bundle, to paper slip, back to bundle. That much of the report is real.

**Why it is not major:**
- **The script allows a single leaf.** Script 5.5 says Ramayyan is "lowering the leaf" and 6.3 says Varma is "reading the leaf". Ramayyan broke the wax in 5.3, so an opened ola showing one leaf fits the script.
- **The real faults are small:**
  1. The 5.5 slip is shaped and coloured like paper instead of a long, narrow palm leaf.
  2. 6.1 shows the bundle tied up again after it was opened.
- **The no-writing complaint does not hold.** The marks on the 5.5 slip, and the similar ones on the 6.3 leaf, are faint rows of texture lines. There are no letter shapes. Old palm-leaf letters naturally have scratched rows like this, and the script's no-text rule is about avoiding legible lettering.
- **The prop is tiny at print size.** On the 5.5 page it is about 115 by 50 pixels out of 1838 across, roughly half an inch wide on a 6 by 9 inch page. In 6.1 the bundle is also small.

**Fix if wanted:** in 5.5, make the slip a long, narrow, brown palm leaf to match 6.3; or in 6.1, show the leaf being handed over instead of the tied bundle.

confirmed.description: The coin business set up in 5.3 is missing. The brass tray of gold coins is not on the table, and Nagoji is not setting a coin on a stack. The background has also changed from the open, sea-facing hall to a closed plaster wall with a cream banner and a spear rack.
confirmed.evidence: The table holds only palm-leaf bundles and a small pot, and the big balloon covers the area where his hands would be. 7.2 and 7.5 show the coin tray on the same low table, and every other hall panel (5.3, 6.2, 6.5, 7.2, 7.4, 7.5) is open to the sea.

verdict.reason: Confirmed as major, but the cause is the lettering and the crop, not the drawing. The raw frame (chapters/ch12/frames/page-07-panel-03-v01.png) has the whole beat: Nagoji's right hand setting a gold coin on a small stack, the brass tray of coins beside it on the low table, and the sea through the open left side of the hall. On the printed page (renders/r2/page-07.png, panel 7.3), the panel is cropped from about 1536 px to about 1205 px wide, which cuts off most of the left side where the sea is. The second Nagoji balloon ("The Marathas are patient...") then sits right over the hand, the coin stack and the tray. I mapped the frame coordinates onto the page: the stack lands at about x310, y445 and the tray at about x354-475, y470-505, both inside the balloon. So a reader sees only the palm-leaf bundles, the ink pot and a scroll on the table. This loses the business the script plants in 5.3 so that 7.3 can show what a pagoda is (script note under "War hall"). It also ignores the prompt's instruction to keep the lettering on the clear upper wall, "away from his hand and the stack of coins". The second complaint, about the background, only partly holds. The cream banner, spear rack and plaster wall are in the source art too, and the crop is what hides the open sea side. That wall is a small break from 6.5, which shows open sea behind Nagoji's pillar, but it is minor by itself. This is clearly wrong but localized, and it can be fixed without new art: move or shrink the second balloon onto the empty upper-right wall, and shift the crop left so the hand, stack and tray show. It is not a blocker because the dialogue still carries the story beat.

confirmed.description: The ola handover is not drawn. Varma's hands are empty in his lap, and Ramayyan holds a stylus at his chest. He does not take the ola from Varma or tuck it into his cloth, so the prop Varma was holding in 7.2 simply disappears.
confirmed.evidence: 7.2: Varma holds the tied leaf bundle up. 7.4: no leaf anywhere in frame, and Ramayyan's right hand holds a thin stylus.

verdict.reason: I'm confirming this, but as minor rather than major. Page 7, panel 7.4: I zoomed in and no ola appears anywhere in the frame. Varma's left hand rests empty on the seat by the red cushion, and his right hand is hidden behind Ramayyan's balloon. Varma is not shown handing anything over. Ramayyan is tucking a thin stick, a stylus, into the fold of his white cloth at his chest. In panel 7.2 Varma clearly holds a flat, tied leaf bundle, so the prop the script calls for (script lines 235 and 315: "business with the ola and the coins") is never handed over and simply disappears. Nothing in the bible or script excuses this. It stays minor for three reasons. First, Ramayyan's tucking gesture is drawn and fits his bible kit (CONTINUITY line 91: palm-leaf bundles and stylus), so at print size the panel reads roughly as he tucks something away, close to the scripted business. Second, Varma's empty hands in a new shot read naturally as him having set the ola down. Third, the dialogue, speakers and story beat (Ramayyan's "window" line leading into Varma rising in 7.5) all land, with no identity or costume error. It is a small prop and staging loss, not a clear localized error. The fix, if wanted, is to replace the stylus in Ramayyan's hand with the tied ola bundle.

confirmed.description: The irons on Chanda Sahib's wrists, which pay off 'have him in chains' from 6.1, cannot be seen, and the coin-counting cloth is almost entirely hidden. The two caption boxes sit over the captive's lower body and the cloth.
confirmed.evidence: The captive (cream turban, beard, face in shadow, soiled white jama) is visible only from the chest up. The left caption covers his arms and lap, and only a few coins show under the right caption.

verdict.reason: The problem is real. In the unlettered frame (chapters/ch12/frames/page-08-panel-03-v01.png), the captive clearly wears wrist manacles joined by a hanging chain, at about frame x 610-750, y 550-680. A wide white cloth of coins with stacked columns sits in front of him. The script asks for both ("iron at his wrists", officers who "count coin on a cloth before him"), and the irons are what pay off "have him in chains" from 6.1. In the r2 page-08 render, the left caption ("And now, without knowing it...") sits right over the captive's forearms, hands and lap, so the manacles and chain are completely hidden. The right caption ("The world turns strangely...") covers most of the coin cloth and the stacks. Only a thin strip of loose coins shows between and under the two boxes, plus one officer's hand holding coins. The captive is visible only from the chest up (turban, shadowed bearded face, soiled jama shoulders). At print size he reads as a seated bearded man, not as a prisoner. The bible (Chanda Sahib, ch11-12: "seen only backlit, silhouetted or shadowed") covers the shadowed face but gives no reason to hide the irons. It is major, not blocker: the art is right and only the lettering hides it. Moving the two captions up into the empty dark tent canopy, or to the top-left and top-right corners, would show the irons and the coin cloth without a redraw.

confirmed.description: Chanda Sahib's riders wheeling away across the open scrub are hidden. The second caption box sits right over them, so the enemy, and with it the point of the beat, is missing.
confirmed.evidence: Zoomed under the 'We spoke of it afterward...' caption, only a dust cloud and a few horse legs show at the right edge. No dust-coloured coats or dark turbans are readable anywhere in the panel.

verdict.reason: Confirmed. In the page 4 render, panel 4.1 (top-left), the second caption ("We spoke of it afterward... worthy enemy") covers almost all of the right half of the art. Below the caption you see only a dust cloud and a few dark horse legs. A thin strip at the panel's right edge shows part of one rider: a dust-coloured quilted coat, a dark turban and a grey horse, under 2 mm wide at print size. So the reviewer was slightly wrong to say no coat or turban shows anywhere, but nothing a reader could recognise as Chanda Sahib's cavalry wheeling away is visible. I checked the source frame chosen in SELECTION-MANIFEST-r2 (chapters/ch12/frames/page-04-panel-01-v03.png). It draws the script beat correctly: a full column of about ten riders in dust-coloured quilted coats and dark indigo turbans, no green and no red sashes, wheeling away across the red scrub in dust. That whole column sits right where the caption box was placed. As printed, the Nair musketmen and Dhanaji face a cloud of dust, and the "worthy enemy" the caption names is hidden under the caption itself. The script makes these riders the point of the beat ("wheel away from the ravine mouth, faster, refusing the broken ground"), and nothing in the script or the bible allows hiding them. Severity is major rather than blocker: the art is correct, so no redraw is needed. Moving the caption fixes it, for example into the open sky at top centre or right, or stacked under "Near Nagercoil." above the horizon line. The dust, the horse legs and Dhanaji's lines in 4.2 also partly carry the beat.

confirmed.description: Anachronistic footwear. The boots set below the shrine steps are drawn as modern lace-up work or combat boots with rows of eyelets, pull-loops and welted soles. They do not match the cross-wrapped leather boots on Nagoji's commander sheet, and they read as 20th-century in a 1740 scene. The script makes these boots a featured beat.
confirmed.evidence: Crop of page-02.png at about x150-500, y820-1050. A pair of brown boots stands on the ground at the bottom-left of the panel, with criss-cross laces through eyelets and a heel pull-tab on each. Compare the cross-laced, wrapped boots in 4.2 (page-04 at about x1200-1690, y900-1115) and on nagoji-v2.png.

verdict.reason: Confirmed, and it stays major. The boots on page 2, panel 1 are at about x150-330, y880-1010 in page-02.png. Zoomed in, they look like modern lace-up service or work boots: a straight row of eyelets up the front, tight criss-cross laces, a stitched toe cap, a welted sole with a squared heel, and a pull-loop at the back of each shaft. They do not match the approved commander sheet (V13 concepts/nagoji-v2.png). The sheet shows soft, slouched boots with the lacing wrapped around the shaft. Page 4, panel 2 of this chapter (page-04.png at about x1200-1690, y900-1115) draws them correctly, so on page 2 they are both off-model and anachronistic for 1740. Nothing in the bible or script allows this. CONTINUITY.md for ch12 @2-3 only says "boots together below the shrine steps", and script 2.1 makes the boots-off a deliberate beat ("His boots are off and set side by side on the ground below the bottom step"). At print size they cover about 0.6 x 0.55 inches in the lower left of the panel, the only footwear in it and a featured object. The front eyelet lacing and toe caps are still clear in a 1:1 crop of the panel, so the problem is not too slight to matter. It is a localized costume error and anachronism, not an identity error, so major rather than blocker. Fix: redraw the pair to match the sheet's wrapped, cross-laced boots, with no eyelet row, pull-loops or toe-cap stitching.

confirmed.description: The action is hidden. The 'We spoke of it afterward...' caption covers the open scrub where Chanda Sahib's riders should be wheeling away from the ravine mouth. As placed, the panel shows only Nagoji, Dhanaji and the Nair musketmen aiming at nothing, so the beat (the enemy refusing the broken ground) is lost.
confirmed.evidence: Crop of page-04.png at about x150-915, y480-995. The right half of the panel is the caption box. Only a sliver of a horse leg and dust shows at the extreme right edge, and no enemy riders are readable anywhere.

verdict.reason: I confirmed this on page 4, panel 1. The script (4.1) calls for Chanda Sahib's riders out on the open scrub, wheeling away from the ravine mouth in quilted coats and dark turbans. The selected source art, chapters/ch12/frames/page-04-panel-01-v03.png, does draw that: a band of about 10 riders in the dust, in the middle-right of the frame at roughly art x 950-1530, y 420-620. On the lettered page-04.png (crop x 145-920, y 475-1000), the 'We spoke of it afterward with the frustrated respect of men who had faced a worthy enemy.' caption box covers almost exactly that region. All that is left is a sliver of one rider and a horse at the extreme right edge, plus some horse legs and dust under the box's bottom edge. So the panel reads as Nagoji, Dhanaji and the Nair musketmen aiming at empty scrub, and the beat of the enemy refusing the broken ground is lost. The bible and script give no allowance for this. The art itself is correct; the fault is only in where the caption was placed, and it could go over the sky at the top right or the rocks at the top left instead. That makes it a localized major, not a blocker needing a redraw.

confirmed.description: The captive's irons are hidden. The 'And now, without knowing it...' caption sits over the seated Chanda Sahib's lap and hands, so the iron at his wrists, which is what makes him read as 'the rider fallen', cannot be seen. As drawn he reads as a seated noble at a coin count.
confirmed.evidence: Crop of page-08.png at about x425-1415, y1235-1815. The turbaned, bearded figure in the white jama at the centre is visible only down to the chest. The left caption box covers everything below, and no manacles are visible anywhere in the panel.

verdict.reason: Confirmed, but it is a lettering-placement fault, not an art fault. On the lettered page (page-08.png, panel 8.3 at about x424-1418, y1235-1815), the captive in the white jama and cream turban is visible only from the turban down to the upper chest. The left caption ("And now, without knowing it...") covers his lap and hands, and no iron shows anywhere in the panel. The source frame (chapters/ch12/frames/page-08-panel-03-v01.png) does draw the beat clearly: heavy iron cuffs on both wrists and a chain hanging across his lap, at about frame x600-760, y540-680. So the art follows the script ("iron at his wrists"), and the caption placement hides it. What stays visible (no jewel on the turban, a speckled and soiled jama, face in shadow, officers counting coin) reads as a seated noble at a coin count, not as a prisoner. The second caption's "One man's capture" helps but does not say who is captive. The adaptation notes rely on this panel to show "the rider fallen" against 1.3. The right caption also covers most of the coin cloth. Severity is major, not blocker: the panel needs no redraw. Moving the left caption up into the empty dark tent canopy (top centre of the panel) or to the far left over the seated officer's back would uncover the chained wrists.

confirmed.description: The business is hidden. The large 'The Marathas are patient...' balloon covers Nagoji's hands, the low table and the brass coin tray. The scripted action of setting one gold coin on a stack, which pays off the tray planted in 5.3, cannot be seen.
confirmed.evidence: Page-07.png panel 3 (right half of the second tier). Only Nagoji's head shows between the two balloons. The lower balloon fills the table area from about x1090-1500, y1210-1490 (original pixels), and no coin or tray is visible.

verdict.reason: The problem is real. I zoomed into the full-resolution crop of page 7, panel 3 (about x920 to 1690, y920 to 1580). The lower balloon ("The Marathas are patient...") sits over Nagoji from the chin down to the floor. It hides his chest, both hands and the middle of the low table. The only things visible on the table are a palm-leaf bundle and a brass ink pot on the left and a rolled leaf on the right, with no coin, stack or brass tray anywhere. Below the balloon you can see only the edge of his white cloth and red sash. The script (7.3) calls for Nagoji "setting one plain gold coin on a small stack from the brass tray". The script notes say the tray planted in 5.3 "lets 7.3 show what a pagoda is", and the checklist line "7.2 to 7.4: business with the ola and the coins" counts it as a beat. That business never appears on the page. Neither the bible nor the script allows dropping it. It is major rather than a blocker for three reasons: the dialogue still reads clearly, the coin tray does appear in 7.2 (on the side table) and in 7.5, and the fix is local (move or shrink the balloon, or redraw this one panel with the hands and coin clear of the lettering).

confirmed.description: The page does not read as a coherent comic grid. Every row is a different width and centred, so the page steps in and out like a pyramid, unlike the clean full-width grid of approved Ch1 p1. Panel 8.2 is squeezed to under half the live width, and its caption has to stack into a tall 8-line column that fills about 45% of the panel.
confirmed.evidence: Measured row extents in the 1838x2775 render: the live width elsewhere is x 148-1688. Here 8.1 is x 316-1516, 8.2 is x 572-1260 (688 px), 8.3 is x 420-1412, 8.4 is x 384-1448 and 8.5 is x 192-1640. In 8.2 the caption 'I had fled the Peshwa's justice...' runs to 8 lines, with a dark sliver between the box and the right border.

verdict.reason:
I'm confirming this as a real problem, but I'm downgrading it from major to minor.

What I confirmed: I measured the rows on page 8 (1838x2775) and the reviewer's numbers hold. Rows on the other pages span x 140-1680. On page 8:
- 8.1 spans x 300-1500
- 8.2 spans x 560-1260, about 700 px or 45% of the column
- 8.3 spans x 420-1400
- 8.4 spans x 380-1440
- 8.5 spans x 180-1640

Every row is inset and centred, so the page steps in and out like a pyramid. No other page in the chapter does this to the same degree. Pages 1, 2, 3 and 5 fill the full width, and pages 4, 6 and 7 inset at most one or two rows. The 8.2 caption does stack into 8 lines in a narrow box that covers the right 40-45% of the panel.

Why not major:
1. The pipeline accepts narrower centred panels as a normal result. Its README says many 3:2 frames "come out narrower than the column," and page 8's rows were set by hand from planner-verified minimum heights (the notes in LAYOUT-fitted-s1m2.json).
2. The script's only layout cue for this page is 8.5, "Full width, bottom." That row spans about 94% of the column, just under the pipeline's 95% target, which a reader cannot see.
3. Nothing is unreadable or missing. The 8.2 caption is large and clear, and it does not cover Nagoji's figure, the smoke or the coastline. All five beats are intact.
4. The "dark sliver" between the 8.2 caption and the right border is about 6 px (x 1251-1260), roughly 0.5 mm at print size, so it is negligible.

The remaining issue is visual polish. The page looks ragged next to its siblings, and 8.2 is cramped. Pairing 8.2 with 8.4 in one row, or widening 8.2, would fix it.

confirmed.description: The page grid is ragged and the reading order is ambiguous. Panel 4.1 starts about 120 px lower than 4.2 and leaves an empty cream gap above it, so the 4.2 caption 'Dhanaji admitted it.' is the highest lettering on the page and a reader may start there before 'Near Nagercoil.' Rows 4.4 and 4.5 are inset by different amounts and do not line up with each other or with the full-width 4.3.
confirmed.evidence: 4.2 artwork begins at y~358 and 4.1 at y~480; only 4.2 is present across y 358-479 (x 920-1688). 4.4 spans x 388-1444 and 4.5 spans x 248-1584, while 4.3 spans x 148-1688.

verdict.reason:
The measurements are right, but this is polish, not a major problem. I measured page 4 with Pillow. Panel 4.2's border starts at y=358 and runs to 1116. Panel 4.1 runs from y=480 to 994, so it is centered vertically against 4.2. That leaves a cream gap of about 122 px above and below 4.1, roughly 0.4 in at print size. Rows 4.4 (x 391-1446) and 4.5 (x 251-1585) are each centered at a different width under the full-width 4.3 (x 148-1688).

The claim that the reading order is ambiguous does not hold. Panel 4.1 sits entirely inside 4.2's vertical band and to its left, so the normal left-to-right reading within a tier puts it first. Its captions also lead straight into 4.2's 'Dhanaji admitted it.' Starting on that caption would be odd, but a reader would sort it out at once.

The uneven insets are not specific to this page. The layout engine centers narrower rows on several pages of this chapter: page 6 (x 240-1596), page 7 (225-1612 and 240-1597) and page 8 (319-1518, 386-1450, 195-1642). Page 7 also has offset top edges within a row, though only by about 37 px.

What is worth fixing is the visible empty gap above 4.1 and the unbalanced tier. Top-aligning 4.1 with 4.2, or cropping 4.1 to fill the row height, would fix it. The script also marks 4.5 as 'Full width', but it is drawn inset at x 251-1585 rather than spanning 148-1688. Both are minor fixes.

confirmed.description: The caption 'We spoke of it afterward with the frustrated respect...' sits over the open scrub where Chanda Sahib's riders wheel away from the ravine mouth. That is half of the panel's action, and the caption hides it.
confirmed.evidence: Zoomed crop: only a sliver of one rider shows at the caption's right edge, plus horse legs and dust below its bottom edge (around x 880-900, y 600-800 in the original). The rest of the enemy cavalry is behind the box.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 4, panel 1. I compared the lettered page with the unlettered source frame, chapters/ch12/frames/page-04-panel-01-v03.png. The source frame shows a clear column of about ten of Chanda Sahib's riders: dust-coloured quilted coats, dark indigo turbans, talwars raised. They wheel away across the open red scrub on the right side of the panel, roughly 60 to 98 percent across and 40 to 60 percent down. On the page (page-04.png, crop at original x 520-925, y 540-1005), the second caption box, "We spoke of it afterward with the frustrated respect of men who had faced a worthy enemy.", sits exactly over that band. What remains visible: one partial rider at the panel's right edge, a few horse legs, and the dust under the box's bottom edge. The script (4.1) makes the riders who wheel away, "faster, refusing the broken ground", half of the panel's action. That is the visual setup for Dhanaji's lines in 4.2 about their faster horse and letting the land fight. Neither the script nor the bible allows hiding them. Reletter 8.3 so the captions sit in the empty dark tent canopy at the top of the panel, or reframe the crop, so the wrist irons and the coin cloth show.

refuted.description: Pseudo-text is painted into the art. The leaf Ramayyan lowers while saying 'Chanda Sahib has fallen' is ruled with columns of writing-like lines. This breaks the no-text rule. It is also a flat paper-like sheet, not the corded, wax-sealed ola bundle shown in 5.2 and 6.1.

Severity "major" is not justified, and the finding is refuted as too slight to matter at print size.

Protection money is what it was" balloon crosses his head only about 23 px at full resolution above his eyebrows, with its tail running down between his eyes. The CONTINUITY.md line for Ramayyan (receding hair) and script 2.4 are not broken by anything visible here.

refuted.description: Ramayyan's identity drifts within the temple-steps scene. In 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1 he matches the sheet: balding crown, receding hair. **Panel 2.4.** In the page render, the "He had no choice..." balloon covers the top of Ramayyan's head. Its bottom edge and tail sit right on his brow. refuted.description: Varma's beat, leaning forward from his seat as Ramayyan hands him the leaf, is hidden. The 'Captured...' balloon fills the space between Ramayyan's outstretched hands and Varma, so the receiving king shows only as a head peeking out beside a pillar, and the handoff never lands.
